notes.text: This case study examines shared kernel data in xv6 on four CPUs. Team names and roll numbers follow the supplied division document. Faculty, semester, and academic year remain blank for the department to complete. I’ll begin with the race definition, then trace the allocator example.

title: Problem Statement and Introduction

elements.name: Rectangle 1
elements.text: Problem Statement and Introduction

elements.name: Rectangle 3
elements.text: Problem: study concurrent access to shared kernel data without synchronization.

elements.name: Rectangle 4
elements.text: Analyze how xv6 locks prevent inconsistent updates.

elements.name: Rectangle 5
elements.text: Objectives: understand critical sections, identify shared data, explain mutual exclusion, observe concurrent updates, and explain lock safety.

elements.name: Rectangle 6
elements.text: Activities: stress test, remove/restore four lock calls, compare. Outcome: explain lock safety. Source: Case Study 14 brief.

elements.name: Rectangle 5
elements.text: Motivation: four CPUs share one allocator, so concurrent kalloc() and kfree() calls can overlap.

notes.text: The assignment studies xv6 shared kernel data and its existing locks. The project compares original locking, a temporary four-call removal, and restoration. The motivation is that multiple CPUs can request and release physical pages concurrently. Next I’ll show how two CPUs can interleave the same free-list update. Say clearly: this slide is the problem statement, objectives and motivation.

title: 1. Race conditions depend on interleaving

elements.name: Rectangle 1
elements.text: 1. Race conditions depend on interleaving

elements.name: Rectangle 3
elements.text: Race condition: shared-data correctness depends on how concurrent operations interleave.

elements.name: Rectangle 4
elements.text: In xv6, concurrent kalloc() calls can read the same kmem.freelist head.

elements.name: Rectangle 5
elements.text: Table 1. A stale free-list head can assign page P twice

elements.name: Table 6
elements.text:
Step	CPU 0: kalloc()	CPU 1: kalloc()
1	r0 = freelist = P	r1 = freelist = P
2	freelist = P->next	freelist = P->next
3	return P	return P

elements.name: Rectangle 7
elements.text: Source: xv6 kernel/kalloc.c. Illustrative schedule, not a recorded trace.

notes.text: A race is a correctness defect whose outcome depends on how concurrent operations interleave. The xv6 example is the allocator: without kmem.lock, CPU 0 and CPU 1 can both read P as the free-list head, both advance the head from the same stale pointer, and both return P. This is a source-level possible schedule, not a trace claimed for any one recorded failure. That stale update can cause memory corruption, allocator failures, or a kernel trap.

title: 2. Race conditions can corrupt data and stop kernel work

elements.name: Rectangle 1
elements.text: 2. Race conditions can corrupt data and stop kernel work

elements.name: Rectangle 3
elements.text: A lost head update can make a free page unreachable.

elements.name: Rectangle 4
elements.text: Two allocators may return the same physical page.

elements.name: Rectangle 5
elements.text: Broken links can corrupt memory or trap the kernel.

elements.name: Rectangle 6
elements.text: Damage can spread into unrelated processes and kernel work.

elements.name: Rectangle 7
elements.text: Source: allocator invariant. A timeout alone is not a deadlock diagnosis.

notes.text: The allocator invariant requires each free physical page to appear exactly once in the free list and never be returned to two callers at once. Violating that invariant can lose pages, corrupt memory, or crash the kernel. A race and a deadlock describe different problems. Before the proposed fix, I’ll review the existing xv6 locks and their tradeoffs.

title: Existing System: xv6 protects a global free list

elements.name: Rectangle 1
elements.text: Existing System: xv6 protects a global free list

elements.name: Rectangle 3
elements.text: Table 2. Shared kernel structures and their locks

elements.name: Table 4
elements.text:
Shared structure	Lock and purpose
Physical-page free list	kmem.lock — serializes kalloc() and kfree()
Process table	p->lock — protects per-process state
PID allocator	pid_lock — coordinates PID assignment
Parent/child state	wait_lock — coordinates wait transitions
Buffer cache	bcache.lock — protects shared metadata
Timer ticks	tickslock — protects the shared tick count

elements.name: Rectangle 5
elements.text: Source: MIT xv6 locking chapter. Per-CPU lists need refill/steal; CAS needs ABA-safe reclamation; neither was tested.

elements.name: Rectangle 5
elements.text: Drawbacks: one global lock makes CPUs spin under contention.

notes.text: Standard xv6 uses one global kmem.lock for a single physical-page free list. This is simple and correct but serializes allocators and can make CPUs spin under contention. Per-CPU free lists can reduce that contention but need page refill or stealing logic. A lock-free compare-and-swap path needs safe pointer handling, including ABA mitigation. These alternatives were not implemented or benchmarked. Other shared structures listed here were reviewed at source level only. Now I’ll state the synchronization rule this experiment tests. Drawbacks of the existing design: contention on the single global lock, and the alternatives need extra complexity.

title: 3. Proposed Solution: hold kmem.lock for the full update

elements.name: Rectangle 1
elements.text: 3. Proposed Solution: hold kmem.lock for the full update

elements.name: Rectangle 3
elements.text: Keep kmem.lock around each free-list update.

elements.name: Rectangle 4
elements.text: Protect the complete read-and-update sequence.

elements.name: Rectangle 5
elements.text: Use atomic ownership with acquire/release ordering.

elements.name: Rectangle 6
elements.text: Keep the critical section short.

elements.name: Rectangle 7
elements.text: Source: xv6 allocator code. The experiment restores the existing lock.

notes.text: The solution preserves the invariant by serializing the complete free-list push or pop. In the tested xv6 revision, acquire and release use atomic operations with acquire and release ordering. The experiment restores the existing lock rather than adding a new one. Next I’ll define synchronization and place spinlocks among the common mechanisms.

title: 4-5. Synchronization coordinates shared access

elements.name: Rectangle 1
elements.text: 4-5. Synchronization coordinates shared access

elements.name: Rectangle 3
elements.text: Synchronization coordinates concurrent operations so shared state stays correct.

elements.name: Rectangle 4
elements.text: A critical section protects dependent reads and writes as one operation.

elements.name: Rectangle 5
elements.text: Types: mutex, spinlock, semaphore, condition variable, reader-writer lock, barrier, atomic.

elements.name: Rectangle 6
elements.text: xv6 uses a spinlock for the allocator; this study tests that lock.

elements.name: Rectangle 7
elements.text: Source: xv6 spinlock.c. Atomic ownership excludes other CPUs.

notes.text: Synchronization coordinates concurrent operations so shared state stays correct. A critical section groups dependent reads and writes. Common mechanisms include mutexes, spinlocks, semaphores, condition variables, reader-writer locks, barriers, and atomic operations. The experiment evaluates only xv6’s allocator spinlock. The workflow connects the guest allocation path to the host experiment phases.

title: 6. xv6 holds kmem.lock across each free-list update

elements.name: Rectangle 1
elements.text: 6. xv6 holds kmem.lock across each free-list update

elements.name: Rectangle 3
Rectangle 4
elements.text: Figure 2. kalloc() and kfree() update the free list inside kmem.lock. Source: kernel/kalloc.c.

notes.text: kernel/kalloc.c declares kmem.freelist and kmem.lock. kalloc acquires the lock before reading the head and advancing it. kfree acquires it before linking a page to the head. kernel/spinlock.c and spinlock.h implement initlock, acquire, release, holding, push_off, and pop_off. Source: https://github.com/mit-pdos/xv6-riscv/blob/f780d7850765d74cbdcd1fff4b822d8829f7c9bd/kernel/kalloc.c and https://github.com/mit-pdos/xv6-riscv/blob/f780d7850765d74cbdcd1fff4b822d8829f7c9bd/kernel/spinlock.c The allocator code identifies the protected section; next I’ll explain the guest test.

title: 7. race_test.c checks concurrent page allocations

elements.name: Rectangle 1
elements.text: 7. race_test.c checks concurrent page allocations

elements.name: Rectangle 3
elements.text: The parent forks four workers, waits for all four, then writes one gate token per child.

elements.name: Rectangle 4
elements.text: Each worker requests eight pages, fills a child-specific tag, rereads 32 KiB, then shrinks.

elements.name: Rectangle 5
Rectangle 6
elements.text: Any pipe/fork error or non-zero wait() status makes the run fail.

elements.name: Rectangle 7
elements.text: Source: user/race_test.c; four workers repeat 200 rounds.

notes.text: The guest C program uses a pipe as a start gate, forks four children, and only releases them after all workers exist. Each worker repeats 200 rounds of sbrk(8*4096), writes a unique byte tag across the 32 KiB allocation, waits briefly in user space, rereads each byte, then calls sbrk(-bytes). The parent verifies every wait() status. volatile requests fresh reads in this test; it does not synchronize the kernel or prevent aliasing of a physical page. The guest test creates overlapping allocation requests; next I’ll show the host runner.

title: 8. Removing kmem.lock permits duplicate pages or lost frees

elements.name: Rectangle 1
elements.text: 8. Removing kmem.lock permits duplicate pages or lost frees

elements.name: Rectangle 3
elements.text: Table 4. Possible kalloc() schedule without kmem.lock

elements.name: Table 4
elements.text:
Step	CPU 0	CPU 1
1	Read head P	
2		Read head P
3	Set head to P.next	
4		Set head to P.next
5	Return P	Return P

elements.name: Rectangle 5
elements.text: Source: kernel/kalloc.c. A matching kfree() lost-head update can make a page unreachable.

notes.text: Without kmem.lock, two CPUs can read the same free-list head P before either advances it, and both may return P. During concurrent frees, CPU 0 may link page A to old head F while CPU 1 links page B to F and overwrites the head with B, losing A. These are source-level possibilities. The logs do not identify an exact internal interleaving. The possible schedule motivates the locked baseline shown next.

notes.text: The experimental variant comments out acquire and release in both kalloc() and kfree(), four calls total. The free-list operations and workload stay unchanged. Removing the calls also removes their local interrupt-handling effects when no outer lock is active, so the experiment does not isolate those effects. The source change removes the lock around the full update; next is B02 evidence.

notes.text: The experiment connects a shared-data invariant to mutual exclusion. Locked and restored conditions completed all ten attempts in each dataset, while each unlocked condition produced ten non-PASS outcomes. The conclusion applies to this xv6 revision, QEMU setup, and workload. More CPU counts, allocator-specific lost-page checks, contention measurements, and other shared structures remain future work. The conclusion is limited to this workload; the final slide lists its sources.
